verdict.summary: Every security-relevant operation in pixlet_decode_frame carries a protective statement: pktsize is bounded before any header consumption, width/height are bounded before FFALIGN such that no signed overflow is reachable, and all allocation/decode return statuses are checked. The comparison executes in unsigned arithmetic, so negative int widths (be32 values above INT_MAX) become huge unsigned values and are also rejected; the admitted set is [0, INT_MAX - (1U<<(NB_LEVELS+1))]. FFALIGN adds (1U<<(NB_LEVELS+1))-1, so the maximum aligned result is INT_MAX-1 and no signed overflow occurs. The guard constrains the identical variables with no intervening assignment and executes on every path before the sink (BREAK passes).

Decisive protective statement for all header bytestream consumption (lines 10-54): it admits only pktsize in [45, avpkt->size], so the 44-byte fixed header (reads/skips ending at offset 44) lies fully within the packet, and pktsize-4 cannot underflow. bytestream2_get*/bytestream2_skip additionally clamp to the buffer end by standard semantics. No reaching path reads past the packet (BREAK passes).

assumptions: NB_LEVELS is a small compile-time constant so (1U << (NB_LEVELS + 1)) is a small power of two (value 5 in the actual Pixlet codec).
AVFrame/AVCodecContext/AVPacket/frame and got_frame pointers are valid per the decoder API contract; the fragment contains no NULL producer for them.
bytestream2_get_be32/le32 and bytestream2_skip never read out of bounds by standard semantics (they clamp the position and return 0 on overread).

assumptions: waitpid's standard semantics: fills `status` only on success and returns -1 with errno set (EINTR, ECHILD, EINVAL) on failure; the fragment retries only EINTR.

evidence.reason: len is produced at line 31 (bytestream2_get_be16u into int) with residual range 0..65535 and no shown minimum; guards at lines 8 and 29 check only that 2 bytes remain in the stream (bytes_left), not the magnitude of len, so they admit len=0/1 (wrong-object drift: constrained value is bytes_left, consumed value is len). With len=0, len - 2 = -2 converts to 0xFFFFFFFE at bytestream2_skip's unsigned size parameter, moving the read cursor far beyond the finite codestream buffer, making subsequent byte reads out of bounds (CWE-195 primary, CWE-125 secondary). The post-check at line 64 evaluates after the skip and cannot undo it. Absent fix: validate len >= 2 immediately after line 31 (e.g., if (len < 2) return AVERROR(EINVAL);).

Independent second copy of the same sink in the default branch: the same unvalidated len from line 31 (range 0..65535, no minimum) reaches len - 2; len=0/1 yields -2/-1, converted to ~4 GiB at the unsigned skip parameter, advancing the cursor past the buffer end for subsequent out-of-bounds reads. Guards at lines 8/29 admit these values, the post-check at line 64 runs after the sink, and no len >= 2 check exists on this path. Absent fix: validate len >= 2 before the switch.

bytestream2_skip consumes an unsigned size per the standard FFmpeg bytestream API, so the negative int is converted to a huge unsigned value.

limitations: s->tile + s->curtileno (line 16) and s->tile[s->curtileno] (lines 50-52): no in-fragment capacity for s->tile and no shown bound on curtileno, demoted for lack of capacity evidence.

verdict.summary: The user-provided directory path is concatenated into a shell command executed via popen without any sanitization or validation, so shell metacharacters in dir_path (e.g. ';', '|', '$(...)') are interpreted by /bin/sh, enabling arbitrary command injection.

evidence.reason: Command injection at the popen sink (CWE-78): command is built at line 16 as "ls -l " + dir_path, where dir_path is entry-point attacker-controlled data from argv[1] (line 44). The only guards on the path are argc != 2 (line 39), which ensures argv[1] exists but does not constrain its content, and pipe == nullptr (line 20), which is evaluated after the sink and constrains the pipe handle rather than the command text. popen's standard semantics execute the string via /bin/sh -c, so a witness like dir_path = "; cat /etc/passwd" yields command = "ls -l ; cat /etc/passwd", admitted by every guard and reaching the sink unmodified (BLOCK test survives). The absent one-statement fix is validation/sanitization of dir_path rejecting shell metacharacters before concatenation (or substituting an exec-family argv call).

assumptions: popen executes the command string through /bin/sh -c (standard, name-implied semantics).
argc != 2 at line 39 guarantees argv[1] exists but imposes no constraint on its characters.
limitations: The fgetc return value stored in char (line 27) can truncate byte 0xFF or, on platforms with unsigned char, fail to compare equal to EOF causing non-termination; treated as a robustness concern, not the deciding finding.
Downstream effects of injected commands (data exfiltration, file modification) are not shown in the fragment; the injection itself is the confirmed failure.
Directory-not-found or permission-error handling is delegated to popen failure and is not analyzed beyond the shown code.

evidence.reason: Uninitialized read (CWE-457): 'lowbits' is declared at line 7 with no initializer, no shown assignment anywhere, and only 'highbits' is assigned at lines 10-11; the residual (indeterminate) value reaches the sink at line 12 as an argument to getbits, whose write places those bytes into key->data (the auth key, consumed at line 36 with extent 8). limitations: The fragment is a mangled amalgamation (duplicate 'XdmcpGenerateKey' header at line 1, emulate_getrandom_buf body referencing key->data instead of its auth/len parameters); analysis is confined to the shown control flow.
The predictable-seed weakness (CWE-338) is shared by both pair members and is not the discriminating one-statement difference; it is reported only as a confirmed secondary sink.

verdict.summary: chmd_read_headers reads the per-chunk entry count with EndGetI16 (line 184) without any non-negative check, and 'while (num_entries--)' (line 186) iterates for negative counts (up to 2^32 times) while p advances past the chunk_size-byte chunk buffer (allocated line 157), causing deterministic heap out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125) and an effectively unbounded loop (CWE-835); the line-188 guard 'name_len > (unsigned int)(end - p)' is insufficient because once READ_ENCINT has moved p past end, the negative ptrdiff is cast to a huge unsigned value and admits any name_len.

evidence.reason: num_entries is the signed result of EndGetI16(end) (line 184) over the last two attacker-controlled chunk bytes (read at line 165; end set at line 183); 0xFF 0xFF yields -1 with no shown sign check, and the post-decrement condition is true for negative values, so the loop runs ~2^32 iterations (signed wraparound) or until an out-of-bounds read faults. Capacity: chunk_size bytes from sys->alloc at line 157. Missing one-statement fix: 'if (num_entries < 0) goto chunk_end;' (or 'while (num_entries-- > 0)') before the loop. Mechanism: input-driven unbounded iteration count (CWE-835) feeding heap over-reads (CWE-125).

With minimal chunk_size = pmgl_Entries+2 (admitted by line 106), p starts at chunk[pmgl_Entries] == end (lines 182-183); a 0xFF first byte in the num_entries field forces this encint to consume chunk[chunk_size-2], chunk[chunk_size-1], and then chunk[chunk_size] - the first byte past the chunk_size-byte allocation from line 157 - a deterministic heap out-of-bounds read independent of heap contents (CWE-125). The guard at line 188 cannot prevent it because it is evaluated after this read and admits any name_len once end-p is negative (cast to huge unsigned).

Once p has passed end (possible as shown above and after line 191 'p += name_len' under the broken line-188 guard), name points outside the chunk_size-byte allocation while name_len is unconstrained, so this memcpy-style copy reads past the chunk buffer (CWE-125). Guard-Identity Audit: wrong-bound drift (class 3) - the admitted name_len set is computed from a negative difference zero-extended to unsigned, so it no longer matches the remaining in-buffer bytes. This sink is secondary: reaching it also requires the heap byte decoded as section to be 0 or 1 (line 204 continue), whereas the primary line-187 read is heap-independent.

assumptions: The chunk buffer capacity is exactly chunk_size bytes via sys->alloc at line 157; end = &chunk[chunk_size-2] at line 183 points at the two-byte entry-count field at the chunk tail.
EndGetI16 returns a signed 16-bit value (name implies signedness), so 0xFFFF decodes to -1; no sign constraint is shown.
Line 106 admits chunk_size == pmgl_Entries+2 (>= comparison), so p starts at end; the exact numeric value of pmgl_Entries is irrelevant to the witness.
All chunk bytes, including the final two, are attacker-controlled via the file read at line 165.
limitations: Post-first-iteration behavior of the negative-num_entries loop depends on heap bytes (continuation bits/decoded name_len), but the first OOB byte read at chunk[chunk_size] is deterministic, so the finding does not rest on that dependency.

The '::' system-file name comparisons at lines 223-236 can read name[2..] past the name region when name_len is small, but entering that block requires the section encint/value to satisfy section <= 1, which conflicts with the crafted tail bytes; demoted as a same-root candidate.

The int multiplication chm->chunk_size * chm->num_chunks for version < 3 (line 95) can wrap, but the off_t-cast product check at lines 123-126 bounds the same product and no in-fragment sink consumes sec0.offset afterward; not a demonstrated finding.
A negative first_pmgl can wrap the seek arithmetic at line 151, but only yields seek/read error returns in the fragment (no memory sink); not a finding.
The loop's worst case (2^32 iterations) cannot complete without crashing on the heap over-reads; both outcomes (faulting OOB read and unbounded iteration) are confirmed failure modes.

verdict.summary: megasas_enqueue_frame stores the pci_dma_map result into cmd->frame without checking the mapping pointer: on total DMA-map failure the standard dma_memory_map/address_space_map semantics return NULL while leaving the in/out length unchanged, so the only guard, 'if (frame_size_p != frame_size)' at line 17, admits the NULL (wrong-object drift — it constrains the length, not the pointer), and the NULL mapping is handed to the caller as a successfully enqueued command, causing a NULL-pointer dereference when cmd->frame is used.

evidence.reason: pci_dma_map returns NULL on mapping failure (callee standard semantics; frame is an unconstrained guest-supplied address), and on total failure the in/out length frame_size_p is left unchanged at 1024, so the guard at line 17 ('if (frame_size_p != frame_size)') admits the NULL — Guard-Identity drift class (2): it constrains the length, not the mapping pointer. The NULL reaches this unchecked copy on the success path and is returned at line 41; the only cmd->frame NULL check ('if (cmd->frame)' at line 19) sits inside the failure branch and is bypassed. The absent one-statement fix is to add a mapping-result check, e.g. 'if (!cmd->frame || frame_size_p != frame_size)', which would exclude the NULL; mechanism is a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) when the returned command's frame pointer is consumed.

assumptions: MFI_FRAME_SIZE * 16 yields the positive constant 1024 stored in frame_size (lines 6-7); frame_size_p is the in/out length parameter of pci_dma_map and is 1024 at call time.

pci_dma_map/dma_memory_map return NULL on mapping failure and, for a wholly unmapped address, do not modify the in/out length (standard QEMU semantics); the fragment's own failure-branch NULL test at line 19 corroborates that a NULL mapping result is an expected outcome.
megasas_next_frame returns NULL when no free frame is available, which the fragment handles at lines 10-11 before any cmd dereference.
limitations: The actual crash line (dereference of cmd->frame in the unshown caller, e.g., casting it to a frame header) is not displayed in this fragment; per the analysis the admitted NULL reaches an unchecked in-fragment copy and a success return, which is the demonstrated failure (no downstream exploitation needs to be shown).

If a particular QEMU configuration's dma_memory_map instead zeroes the length on total failure, this witness would be blocked by line 17; the standard unchanged-length behavior and the author's line-19 NULL guard indicate the length-unchanged/NULL case is the operative one.

count and context are stored (lines 28-33) but have no in-fragment dangerous consumer, so any downstream use of them is out of scope; partial mappings (frame_size_p < frame_size) are correctly rejected by line 17.

This analysis is purely from the shown fragment; no verdict is based on which member of the fixed/vulnerable pair the code resembles.

Absent fix: delete or conditionalize line 104 so the KRB5KDC_ERR_CLIENT_NAME_MISMATCH status propagates to the return. CWE-754: a security-relevant identity-verification failure status is discarded without action, failing open the PKINIT client-identity check.

assumptions: crypto_retrieve_cert_sans returns 0 with NULL-terminated princs/upns arrays, with upns non-NULL when the certificate has UPN SANs and allow_upn is set (line 21); the fall-through path to line 98 therefore has retval == 0 and upns != NULL.
Lines 13-15/49-51/54-59/82-87/117-120 (DEBUG_SAN_INFO) and lines 32-47 (#if 0) do not execute in the analyzed configuration.
limitations: OOB candidates on princs/upns were demoted: array capacities are established only inside the unshown crypto_retrieve_cert_sans callee, so no in-fragment capacity expression exists (CAPACITY-EVIDENCE RULE).

NULL-deref candidates were demoted: princs[i] (line 53), upns[i] (line 81) and the cleanup loops (lines 108/113) are each guarded in-fragment (lines 53, 73, 107, 112), and no NULL producer for the parameter pointers is shown.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in the data_size computation: `data_size += image->height * offset;` is not preceded by an overflow guard, so attacker-controlled image->height and offset can wrap data_size to a small value, producing an undersized buffer later consumed (e.g. by CreatePixels) and enabling a heap buffer overflow.

A witness image->height≈UINT_MAX/8 (allowed by L88-90) with offset≈4e9 (allowed by L84-86) makes height*offset≈2e18 wrap UINT_MAX, so data_size becomes small; the later guard at L98-100 runs after this wrap and only bounds the header_size+ext_size add, so it cannot detect it. The wrapped data_size is then used as the buffer size passed to CreatePixels (L118) causing an undersized allocation / heap overflow (CWE-787). Absent one-statement fix: `if (image->height > (UINT_MAX - data_size) / offset) RETURN(XpmNoMemory);` before the add at L94.

assumptions: image->ncolors, image->width, image->height, image->cpp are entry-point (attacker-controlled) fields parsed from the XPM image.

limitations: The actual `data = XpmMalloc(data_size)` allocation is not shown in the fragment; the heap-overflow consequence relies on the in-fragment data_size derivation being the allocation size (CWE-787 noted as secondary).

Stray standalone `RETURN(XpmNoMemory);` lines (L93, L95) and duplicated `data_size += image->height * offset;` are treated as the mangled remnant of missing conditional overflow guards, matching the absent-fix analysis.

verdict.summary: hash_certificate uses the broken MD5 algorithm to "securely" hash an attacker-controlled certificate (argv[1]), with no strong-hash substitution or other protective statement, so MD5's feasible collision attacks defeat the hash's integrity purpose.

evidence.reason: The crypto sink at line 25 consumes attacker-controlled cert data (provenance: argv[1] at line 42, no shown content constraint) with MD5, whose standard semantics are a broken 128-bit collision-prone hash for security use despite the documented purpose 'Hash the given certificate securely' (lines 7-14). The protective statement that would neutralize this failure set is a strong-hash substitution (SHA-256 via SHA256/SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH); it is absent, and no guard on the reach path (only the unrelated !hex_string check at line 19, a wrong-object drift) constrains the algorithm or input. Mechanism: use of a cryptographically broken hash for security-relevant certificate hashing (CWE-327).

assumptions: cert is non-NULL and NUL-terminated because the shown caller passes argv[1] after the argc != 2 check (lines 37-42).
MD5_DIGEST_LENGTH is 16 and the line-18 allocation of 33 bytes exactly bounds the sprintf writes in the line-28 loop (max touched index 32).
limitations: Unchecked MD5 return value (potential uninitialized hash on a failure path) is demoted: the failing path is inside the unshown callee, and the fragment displays no error branch leaving hash unset.
Downstream consumer of the returned hash is not shown, so the concrete exploit impact of an MD5 collision is not demonstrated in-fragment.
sprintf uses a literal "%02x" format and stays within the quoted 33-byte capacity, so no format-string or OOB finding applies.

verdict.summary: In r_core_anal_type_match, the NULL-able lookup results mopvar (r_anal_get_used_function_var, line 161) and jmpbb (r_anal_fcn_bbget_in, line 243) are passed unchecked into __var_rename and r_anal_block_contains respectively, causing a NULL-pointer dereference when analyzing a crafted binary that exercises the __stack_chk_fail or CMP/CJMP constraint paths.

evidence.reason: mopvar is the unchecked result of the lookup r_anal_get_used_function_var (line 161), whose standard semantics return NULL when no variable is associated with mop->addr (e.g. a canary MOV targeting an untracked stack slot). On the reaching path (lines 156-164) the only guards are `if (mop)` (line 160) and `if (type == R_ANAL_OP_TYPE_MOV)` (line 163); neither constrains mopvar, and the reverse protection scan found no excluding statement, so NULL reaches __var_rename, whose name-implied rename semantics dereference the var object (CWE-476). The absent one-statement fix is `if (mopvar)` before the call; the witness (mopvar == NULL) survives the BLOCK test. This is the deciding ABSENT sink.

jmpbb is the unchecked result of the lookup r_anal_fcn_bbget_in (line 243), which per standard lookup semantics returns NULL when jmp_addr (next_op->jump) is not covered by any block of fcn, e.g. a CJMP target outside the function. Guards on the path constrain only chk_constraint/var/type/next_op (line 238) and jmp_op (line 248), so NULL reaches r_anal_block_contains(jmpbb, jmp_addr), whose contains semantics iterate the block object (CWE-476). The absent one-statement fix is `if (jmpbb)` before the contains call; the witness (jmpbb == NULL) survives the BLOCK test.

assumptions: bsize = R_MAX (64, core->blocksize) (line 17) guarantees bsize >= 64, so the guard at lines 78-80 admits i in [0, bsize-33] and the line-88 read of buf (malloc(bsize), line 31) with length bsize-i >= 33 is fully in bounds.
callee_addr (line 114) is assigned in the same branches (lines 119, 125) that set full_name, so the use at line 141 always reads an initialized value (no CWE-457).

r_anal_get_used_function_var and r_anal_fcn_bbget_in are lookups with standard NULL-on-not-found call-site semantics; both are used everywhere else in the fragment with explicit NULL guards except for mopvar (line 161) and jmpbb (line 243).
limitations: S4: r_read_ble(buf, ..., aop.refptr * 8) at line 279 reads up to aop.refptr*8 bytes from `ut8 buf[256]` (line 277); no shown in-fragment producer can drive refptr >= 32, so the OOB candidate is demoted.
strdup and ht_pp_new_size NULL/OOM paths (lines 41, 46, 62, 130, 135, 188) require allocation failure; no attacker-reachable producer is shown, demoted.
fcn->ninstr * 0xf (line 41) would need ninstr ~= 1.4e8 to overflow int; no shown producer drives that value, demoted.

The dereferencing bodies of __var_rename and r_anal_block_contains are unshown; the failure is imputed from their name-implied use of the object argument per call-site semantics, not from observed callee behavior.
NULL invariants for core->anal->esil->trace->db and core->dbg->trace->ht (lines 38-47) have no in-fragment NULL producer; demoted.
The `i` overwrite by the inner for loop (line 246) is neutralized by the reset guard at lines 78-80 before any buf+i use; recorded here as analyzed, not as a defect.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled argv username/password are interpolated unescaped into an XPath expression (lines 36-38) and evaluated (line 41), enabling XPath injection (auth bypass / data disclosure). Separately, student fields NULL-initialized at lines 65-67 are printed unconditionally with %s at lines 118-120, so an XML record missing a child element passes NULL to printf (UB).

evidence.reason: username/password are argv entry-point inputs with no shown filtering; the query built at lines 36-38 embeds them as '%s' literals in an XPath expression, and xmlXPathEvalExpression at line 41 interprets the result. A witness such as username=password="' or '1'='1" survives the BLOCK test: snprintf performs no escaping and no shown guard constrains the values, so the injected predicate selects the first student and the name/age/citizenship are printed. The absent one-statement fix is parameterization (xmlXPathRegisterVariable with $username/$password) or escaping of single quotes before interpolation; primary CWE-643.

result->name/age/citizenship are initialized to NULL at lines 65-67 and assigned only when a matching child element exists (lines 73-78); an attacker-supplied XML student that matches the query but omits the child element leaves the field NULL, and it is passed to printf("%s", ...) with no per-field NULL check. The absent fix is a NULL check (e.g., if(info->name)) before each print; passing NULL to %s is undefined behavior (CWE-476), secondary to the XPath injection.

assumptions: argv strings are NUL-terminated and attacker-controlled entry-point data (argv[1..3] passed at line 114).
snprintf into xpath_query[256] is size-bounded, so oversized credentials cause truncation, not a buffer overflow.
nodeTab[0] at line 51 is protected by the line 50 check nodesetval && nodeNr > 0, which admits only indices 0..nodeNr-1.
Standard libxml semantics: xmlXPathEvalExpression executes the query; xmlNodeGetContent can return NULL on allocation failure.
limitations: NULL content from xmlNodeGetContent/strdup (lines 72-78) is an OOM-only path not attacker-triggerable under normal execution; treated as robustness, not a separate finding.
printf with NULL for %s is undefined per the C standard but glibc prints "(null)", so the practical impact of the secondary CWE-476 item is low.
XPath injection impact (data disclosure/auth bypass) is confirmed by the fragment's own consumption of the result via the prints at lines 118-120.

OOB candidates (output_samples, msb_sample_buffer, dmix_scale_inv, ch_remap) lack in-fragment capacity evidence and are demoted; the residual negative-shift UB has no memory-safety or security-decision consumer.

An upper-bound OOB witness cannot be established because no capacity for `dca->core.output_samples` appears in the fragment (capacity-evidence rule); the guard survives the BREAK identity/reach tests.

PRESENT (NULL, CWE-476 would be absent): `o` is the nullable result of `find_next_hier_dmix_chset` (line 22), but this dereference executes only inside `if (o) {` (line 44), which excludes NULL on every reaching path. The index `c->hier_ofs + ch` has no in-fragment capacity, so the OOB aspect is demoted.

BREAK tests pass: same local value, no intervening modification, degenerate 0 handled, guard on all paths.

`find_next_hier_dmix_chset` may return NULL, as proven by the fragment's own `if (o)` guard.
`ff_dca_core_map_spkr` returns a valid speaker index or a negative sentinel per its call-site semantics.

`shift` can be negative when `c->pcm_bit_res` is large, making `>> shift` (lines 48, 52) undefined behavior; no memory-safety, injection, or security-decision consumer of the result is shown, so this is recorded as a robustness concern (possible CWE-682/CWE-758 class) rather than a confirmed finding.
`1 << ch` (line 27) is UB only for `ch >= 31`, which requires `c->nchannels > 31`; no such value is derivable from the fragment, so it is not a finding.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled argv[1] (line 33, unbounded) reaches std::regex_match (line 20) against a backtracking regex with overlapping quantifiers ([a-zA-Z0-9.-]+ vs \. and the nested (?:\. [a-zA-Z]{2,})*), so a long dot-heavy email causes catastrophic backtracking; no length cap or time bound is present.

evidence.reason: email derives from entry-point argv[1] (line 33) with no shown length constraint, since the only guard, `if (argc != 2)` (line 29), checks argument count, not email length (wrong-object drift). The regex built at line 16 contains an ambiguous `[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+` overlapping the literal `\.` and a nested quantifier `(?:\. [a-zA-Z]{2,})*`, giving super-linear backtracking on inputs such as "a@" + ".a"*N that are admitted unchanged through lines 29->33->34->20. The absent one-statement fix is a length cap before the match, e.g. `if (email.size() > 254) return std::make_tuple(false, pattern);`. The BLOCK test finds no statement excluding the long input, confirming CWE-1333 regular-expression denial of service.

assumptions: The `argc != 2` check (line 29) guarantees argv[1] exists before it is read at line 33.
std::regex uses a backtracking ECMAScript-style engine, for which overlapping and nested quantifiers exhibit super-linear worst-case matching time.
limitations: The binary is a CLI; ReDoS impact presumes the program can be driven with attacker-supplied long arguments (e.g., invoked by a network-facing service or on untrusted input).
Exact worst-case growth (quadratic vs exponential) depends on the regex engine implementation, but the pattern structure shown admits super-linear backtracking on dot-heavy inputs.
No memory-safety or injection sinks were found: all string/container operations in the fragment are bounds-safe, and the only streamed value `pattern` is a fixed literal.

verdict.summary: Every memory-safety sink in the fragment carries an in-fragment protective statement: key_len is validated (>=16) at line 52 before the 16-byte key copy at line 73; key/data/iv/padded_data/encrypted_data NULL checks (52,59,78,86) plus RAND_bytes (66) and AES_set_encrypt_key (96) status checks gate every use; pad_data allocates data_len+padding (line 10) which covers the memcpy/memset extents and keeps padded_len a multiple of AES_BLOCK_SIZE for AES_cbc_encrypt; all loop indices (135-142, 156-168) are bounded by the same lengths used for allocation.

evidence.reason: 16-byte read of key is PRESENT: guard at line 52 'if (!key || !data || key_len < 16) { return result; }' executes on every path to line 73, excluding key_len < 16 so the admitted key_len >= 16 covers the full copy. BREAK test passes: identity (same key/key_len, no intervening modification), boundary (16 <= key_len), degenerate (key_len == 16 admitted and still in bounds), reach (guard precedes sink on all paths).

evidence.snippet:
memcpy(padded_data, data, data_len);
    memset(padded_data + data_len, (unsigned char)padding, padding);
evidence.reason: Writes to padded_data are PRESENT: allocation at line 12 is sized *padded_len (line 10) = data_len + padding with padding in [1,16]; memcpy covers [0,data_len) and memset covers [data_len, data_len+padding) = [data_len, *padded_len), fully within capacity; degenerate data_len == 0 yields a 0-byte copy and a 16-byte memset into the 16-byte buffer. The data_len + padding wraparound witness is blocked by the shown malloc(data_len) gate at lines 125-127.

CBC processing reads/writes padded_len bytes with both buffers allocated at padded_len (lines 12, 85); padded_len is a multiple of AES_BLOCK_SIZE by construction (line 9: padding = 16 - data_len%16; line 10), so no partial-block overrun. All NULL producers are excluded on every path: key/data (52), iv/key (59), padded_data (78), encrypted_data (86), RAND_bytes failure (66).

assumptions: AES_BLOCK_SIZE is 16 (OpenSSL).
malloc-family failure returns NULL and RAND_bytes failure returns != 1, and each such result is checked before use in the fragment.
AES_set_encrypt_key with a fixed, valid 128-bit key does not fail, so its failure branch is unreachable in practice.
limitations: data_len + padding wraparound in pad_data (line 10) would require data_len near SIZE_MAX, which is blocked by the shown malloc(data_len) gate in main (lines 125-127) and OS argv-length limits; no surviving witness.

sscanf return values at lines 136 and 141 are discarded; invalid hex input leaves key[i]/data[i] indeterminate, which is later read and printed. Robustness/initialization weakness (CWE-457) with no memory-safety consequence, so not a confirmed vulnerability in this fragment.

The AES_set_encrypt_key failure branch (lines 96-102) frees iv/key/encrypted_data without re-NULLing, which would leave dangling non-NULL fields that main's line 147 check would misread as success; unreachable because a 128-bit key cannot trigger failure.
Odd-length key/data hex strings are silently truncated; correct operation requires valid, even-length hex input.

verdict.summary: Every dangerous operation that the shown code can demonstrate resolves PRESENT: the reshape copies and output allocations are return-status checked (L37-38, L86-100, L116-117); scale/offset must exactly match num_channels (L43, L48) and non-empty mean/variance must too (L53, L60); side_input shape must equal the post-reshape x shape actually consumed by the functor (L68), so x and side_input reach the functor with matching element counts. The only unconstrained candidates (empty mean/variance and null side_input reaching the unshown FusedBatchNorm functor bodies, and the in_rows*in_cols product) have failure sets that are not demonstrable from the fragment alone.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(context, side_input->shape() == x.shape(),
                  errors::InvalidArgument(
                      "side_input shape must be equal to input shape: ",
                      side_input->shape().DebugString(),
                      " != ", x.shape().DebugString()));
evidence.reason: Protective shape-equality guard for the side_input/x consumption at L103-113. It constrains the same values later consumed: after the L37 reshape, x.shape() is the shape x has at the functor call, and no shown statement modifies either tensor between L68 and the calls. Admitted set = {shapes equal to the consumed x}, which makes the element counts of x and side_input equal, excluding the shape/count mismatch failure for the combined elementwise consumption. BREAK test: identity, boundary, degenerate, and reach all pass (the guard executes on every has_side_input_ path before the only consumption).

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(context, x.CopyFrom(x, dest_shape),
                  errors::InvalidArgument("Error during tensor copy."));
evidence.reason: Return-status check on the 5D-to-4D reshape copy: Tensor::CopyFrom returns false on element-count mismatch or invalid destination shape, and OP_REQUIRES early-exits the kernel on failure, so a failed reshape can never reach the later GetTensorDim/num_channels/functor uses. The destination product (in_rows*in_cols) is a sub-product of the already-valid x shape and cannot overflow int64. This is the fix form 'return-status check' and it is present verbatim.

evidence.snippet:
context, scale.NumElements() == num_channels,
        errors::InvalidArgument("scale must have the same number of elements "
                                "as the channels of x, got ",
                                scale.NumElements(), " and ", num_channels));
evidence.reason: Channel-count equality guard (mirrored for offset at L48 and for non-empty mean/variance at L53/L60) protecting the per-channel consumption inside the FusedBatchNorm functor at L103-113. num_channels is derived from the reshaped x at L41 before the checks and is not modified between the checks and the functor call, so the admitted set contains only tensors with exactly num_channels elements; a mismatched-element count cannot reach the consumer. BREAK test passes on identity, boundary, degenerate, and reach.

assumptions: has_side_input_ does not change during the call, so the L8 ternary and the L67 branch gate the same NULL/non-NULL side_input value.
context->input() returns valid Tensor objects; a Tensor's shape is valid, so in_rows * in_cols (L35) is bounded by x's total element count and cannot wrap.

x.shape() at L68 is the post-reshape shape (local copy reshaped at L37), which is the shape x has at the functor consumption at L103-113; x_shape (L27) is only used for the output allocation fallback and the final reshape back.
limitations: The bodies of functor::FusedBatchNorm<...> (L103-113) are unshown: whether empty estimated_mean/estimated_variance (admitted by the L52/L59 empty-or-equal gates) or a null side_input is dereferenced/read in a harmful way cannot be established from the fragment, so no in-fragment witness for an OOB inside those callees can be constructed.
The internal dimension mapping of GetTensorDim/ShapeFromFormat for 5D tensors and the cuDNN/Eigen handling of tensor_format_ are unshown; no in-fragment capacity contradiction is derivable from them.
No validation of tensor_format_ compatibility with 5D inputs is present, but no OOB derivation from that absence exists inside the shown code.

The side_input guard at L68 was verified against the post-reshape x; if the comparison had referenced the pre-reshape x_shape instead, a 5D/4D discrepancy could have reached the functor, but the shown L68 uses x.shape() and closes that path.

verdict.summary: The buffer writes in both branches are fully constrained by exact-length guards: the packed branch requires len == 32*RLC_FP_BYTES and writes exactly 4*8*RLC_FP_BYTES bytes; the unpacked branch requires len == 48*RLC_FP_BYTES and writes exactly 2*24*RLC_FP_BYTES bytes. No write exceeds the checked capacity, so no dangerous operation admits an unconstrained value.

evidence.reason: Protective exact-length guard for the packed branch. It admits only len == 32*RLC_FP_BYTES (all other values, including negative and smaller len, throw). The four fp8_write_bin calls write offsets 0, 8, 16, 24 each of 8*RLC_FP_BYTES bytes, totaling exactly 32*RLC_FP_BYTES == len, so the buffer is fully consumed but never exceeded. BREAK test: identity (same len constrains the same buffer), boundary (total write == admitted len), degenerate (negative/zero/short len is excluded by !=), reach (all four calls execute after the throw in the same branch). Resolves PRESENT.

Protective exact-length guard for the unpacked branch. It admits only len == 48*RLC_FP_BYTES. The two fp24_write_bin calls write offsets 0 and 24 of 24*RLC_FP_BYTES bytes each, totaling exactly 48*RLC_FP_BYTES == len, fully consuming the buffer without overflow. BREAK test passes on all four axes. Resolves PRESENT.

assumptions: fp8_write_bin and fp24_write_bin write at most the byte count passed as their len argument (standard name-implied semantics), and write into bin starting at the given pointer.
len is the declared capacity of the buffer bin (int parameter, but both guards force it to the exact total write size).
limitations: The packed branch writes fields of a (a[0][1], a[0][2], a[1][0], a[1][2]) rather than the freshly packed value t computed by fp48_pck(t, a); this is a correctness/logic concern, not a memory-safety or injection issue, and is not classified as a vulnerability.
Any overflow that would occur inside an unshown callee body is not treated as an in-fragment finding; the shown length guards fully constrain the write extents within the fragment.

verdict.summary: Every dangerous operation carries an in-fragment protective statement: the AES key size is validated before the first-16-bytes range construction (line 37), RAND_bytes and AES_set_encrypt_key return statuses are checked, and PKCS7 padding guarantees a nonzero multiple-of-16 input matching the output buffer size, so no unconstrained value reaches a memory or crypto sink.

evidence.reason: Protects the sink at line 42 (std::vector<uint8_t> aes_key(key.begin(), key.begin() + AES_KEY_SIZE)): the guard excludes key.size() in [0,15] (AES_KEY_SIZE=16, line 33), so the admitted size range [16,∞) makes `key.begin() + AES_KEY_SIZE` a valid iterator on every path. BREAK test passes: identity (same `key`, no intervening modification), boundary (16 is admitted and sufficient; 15/0 are excluded), degenerate (empty key throws), reach (check precedes and is unconditional).

Status check on the IV generation: RAND_bytes writes IV_SIZE=16 bytes into the 16-byte `iv` (line 45), so capacity matches the write, and a failure status is not silently consumed — the function aborts instead of encrypting with an invalid IV.

Status check on key expansion: AES_set_encrypt_key's nonzero failure return (128-bit key, AES_KEY_SIZE*8) is handled before `enc_key` is consumed by AES_cbc_encrypt at line 64-71, so a failed key setup cannot be used as success.

assumptions: AES_BLOCK_SIZE is OpenSSL's constant 16, and the only pkcs7_pad call in the fragment passes that literal (line 51), fixing block_size=16.
The return of aes_key is the function's documented contract (`tuple containing: {encrypted data, IV, key used for encryption}`), not a disclosure flaw.
hex_to_bytes invalid/odd input relies on std::stoi/substr semantics; std::invalid_argument and std::out_of_range are caught by main's catch at line 118.
limitations: No dangerous operation resolved ABSENT; no failing witness survived the BLOCK test, so no vulnerability is claimed.
Behavior of unshown OpenSSL internals (AES_cbc_encrypt, RAND_bytes) is taken at its documented standard semantics only.
Crypto policy choices (AES-128-CBC) are contract-level design, not an in-fragment weakness: PKCS7 padding and random IV prevent ECB/zero-IV issues.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled value reaches a dangerous operation. The shell commands passed to system()/popen() are built only from a mkstemp-generated filename (randomized, no shell metacharacters), so there is no command injection. The output buffer in execute_command grows correctly: the doubling guard on total_read >= buffer_size always leaves room for the NUL terminator, so output[total_read]='\0' stays in bounds. All security-relevant statuses (system, execute_command, malloc, realloc) are checked. No memory-safety, injection, or status-handling vulnerability is demonstrable within the fragment.

assumptions: param_filename is produced solely by mkstemp from the fixed template /tmp/tempXXXXXX, replacing the six X's with random alphanumeric characters; it is not attacker-influenced.
The fread buffer invariant total_read < buffer_size holds at loop exit because the buffer is doubled whenever total_read >= buffer_size.
limitations: The fd returned by mkstemp is never closed (resource leak), but it is unused and does not lead to a reachable security failure in the shown fragment.
mkstemp's -1 return is unchecked; on failure the openssl command simply fails and create_dsa_key returns NULL, so no memory-safety or injection consequence is demonstrable.
buffer_size *= 2 overflow would require an unattainably large (>2^62 byte) command output and is not an attacker-drivable derivation here.

verdict.summary: All dangerous operations carry protective statements: the length check at line 58 bounds strlen(argv[1]) to at most 255 before generate_receive_log, keeping every sanitized_msg write (indices 0..255) inside the 256-byte buffer; newline/carriage-return characters are sanitized before the log write; the log entry is built with a bounded snprintf and a literal format; allocation failure is checked.

evidence.reason: Decisive protective bound: rejects strlen(argv[1]) >= 256, admitting length 0..255 on the only shown path into generate_receive_log (line 64). Since sanitized_msg has capacity MAX_MSG_LEN = 256 (line 20), the copy loop (indices 0..len-1, line 21) and NUL write at index len (line 28) reach a maximum index 255 < 256. BREAK test passes on identity, boundary, degenerate (len=0 -> zero iterations), and reach (guard precedes the call on every path).

Log-injection neutralization: every newline and carriage-return byte is replaced with a space before sanitized_msg reaches the log sink at line 45, so attacker-controlled msg content cannot forge log lines (CWE-117 mechanism is absent at the consumer).

Bounded sink substitution: snprintf writes at most MAX_MSG_LEN + 40 = 296 bytes into a 296-byte allocation (line 38); worst-case content is '[' (1) + timestamp (19) + '] Received: ' (12) + sanitized_msg (255) = 288 including NUL, within capacity. Format operand is a literal, so no CWE-134.

assumptions: sanitized_msg has capacity MAX_MSG_LEN = 256 per the declaration at line 20.
timestamp has capacity 20 per the declaration at line 34; '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S' produces 19 characters plus NUL.

verdict.summary: Guest-controlled watchdog preload values (d->timer1_preload/d->timer2_preload) flow unconstrained into signed int64 shift and multiply arithmetic in i6300esb_restart_timer. Capacity evidence is the int64_t declaration at L3: a preload of 2^20 selected at L8, shifted by 15 at L12, gives timeout = 2^35, and get_ticks_per_sec() (~1e9) * 2^35 ≈ 2^65 exceeds INT64_MAX, so the multiplication at L16 wraps (CWE-190). The absent one-statement fix is an overflow-safe substitution, e.g. timeout = muldiv64(timeout, get_ticks_per_sec(), 33000000), or a prior clamp on timeout; the BLOCK test shows no shown statement excludes the witness.

The same unconstrained/wrapped timeout from L16 is added to qemu_clock_get_ns(...) at L18 and consumed as the timer expiry; a negative or wrapped value yields a past/erroneous expiry, so the watchdog timer fires at the wrong time. limitations: The declared widths/types of d->timer1_preload and d->timer2_preload are not shown, so the exact reachable magnitude (and therefore whether the multiply overflows for the real device layout) cannot be proven from this fragment alone; the 2^20 witness rests on that unshown width (fragile boundary), limiting confidence.

verdict.summary: encrypt_data hard-codes a fixed IV for AES-CBC: memcpy(result.iv, "0123456789abcdef", AES_BLOCK_SIZE). Every message encrypted under a reused key shares the same initialization vector, so equal first blocks yield equal ciphertext and chosen/known-plaintext attacks against the first block become possible; no random IV generation exists in the fragment, and the IV is returned to callers as if it were per-message.

evidence.reason: The fixed IV literal installed at line 63 flows unchanged through iv_copy (line 99) into AES_cbc_encrypt (lines 100-101), the crypto sink. Its residual range is a single constant (attacker- and caller-predictable), and no statement in the fragment randomizes, reseeds, or otherwise constrains it, so the predictable-IV failure set is fully admitted. The absent one-statement fix is a random IV initialization, e.g. RAND_bytes(result.iv, AES_BLOCK_SIZE), replacing the fixed memcpy. Mechanism: CBC mode is used with an unvarying initialization vector across encryptions under a caller-supplied, possibly reused key, enabling ciphertext comparison and first-block known-plaintext attacks; primary CWE-329. BLOCK test: the witness (the literal IV) survives — line 99 only copies it, line 100 consumes it, and no guard on the path excludes it.

Severity assumes the returned key may be reused across multiple encrypt_data calls, which the API design (returning key and IV for storage) invites; with a fresh secret key per message the confidentiality impact of the fixed IV is reduced but the predictable-IV property remains.

Absent fix: 'if (inflate(&s->zstream, Z_SYNC_FLUSH) != Z_OK) return -1;' before this return. CWE-754: fail-open status handling.

verdict.summary: qcrypto_cipher_decrypt passes the unvalidated entry-point length 'len' directly to block-cipher decryption calls without checking that it is a multiple of the cipher block size; a non-aligned length (e.g. 15 with a 16-byte block) reaches cbc_decrypt/alg_decrypt, whose block semantics require alignment, enabling out-of-bounds handling in the callee.

evidence.reason: len (size_t parameter, line 4) retains its full declared domain 0..SIZE_MAX; no in-fragment statement constrains it to a multiple of the block size ctx->niv shown as argument at line 15. The ternary at line 14 constrains only the cipher context (wrong-object drift), and the default case (lines 18-21) cannot be reached on this path, so the guard coverage for len is empty. The block-cipher callee's standard, name-implied semantics (cbc_decrypt) require length to be a multiple of the block size and process whole blocks, so a non-aligned value such as len=15 with ctx->niv=16 can drive partial/full-block operations past the end of a len-sized output buffer (and asserts otherwise). Witness len=15 survives the BLOCK test: producer is the unconstrained parameter at line 4, the switch (line 8) and ternary (line 14) neither test nor modify it, and it is passed unchanged at line 16. The absent one-statement fix is an alignment validation before the calls, e.g. 'if (len % ctx->niv != 0) { error_setg(errp, ...); return -1; }'. Primary CWE-787 mechanism: unvalidated length reaching a block-cipher decrypt that writes per-block, enabling an out-of-bounds write.

Resolves the single-byte append at L116: only executed when pos is strictly before string_lim (L61), so the 1-byte read at pos is inside str. BREAK test passes.

Resolves the nomatch tail copy at L123: the guard admits only pos < string_lim, so the appended segment [pos, string_lim) is within str; if pos ever exceeds string_lim (empty-match overshoot at L118), the negative tail is excluded. BREAK test passes.

assumptions: onig_search's name-implied contract with the shown arguments (start=pos, end=range=string_lim) gives successful matches with beg[0] >= pos and end[0] <= string_lim, which bounds the L80-81 pre-match copy and the L113 pos advance.
p == replacement.data()+i is preserved because p and i advance by identical amounts each iteration (L99-100, L103-104).
php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex returns fwd >= 1 per its standard semantics.
limitations: regs from onig_region_new() (L62) is dereferenced at L80/L94-96 without a NULL check (checked only at L129 after use); this is OOM-only, not attacker-driven, so it is treated as a robustness concern rather than a confirmed reachable vulnerability.

On an empty match at the very end of the string, pos can transiently overshoot string_lim by one (L118); it is only passed to onig_search, which returns mismatch under standard semantics, and is never dereferenced in the fragment.
The empty-match break inside `#if moriyoshi_0` (L73-78) is compiled out and not credited; termination is instead guaranteed by the strict per-iteration increase of pos.
A hypothetical fwd == 0 return from php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex would stall the inner loop; no shown producer or standard callee semantics demonstrate that value.

verdict.summary: The only dangerous operation with an in-fragment failure set is the accumulation ibe->outpos += ret and its downstream use in the qemu_chr_fe_write call (outbuf + outpos, outlen - outpos). The guard 'if (ret > 0)' at line 10 unconditionally excludes zero and negative returns (including qemu_chr_fe_write's standard negative-error outcome) before the accumulation, so outpos cannot regress out of range. Overshoot is self-corrected by the outpos >= outlen reset branch before any subsequent write. All remaining OOB candidates (outbuf cap/capacity, outbuf[0..1] writes, entry-state outpos/outlen inconsistency) lack in-fragment capacity or producer evidence and are demoted, so a per-sink ABSENT resolution with a surviving BLOCK-test witness cannot be established.

evidence.snippet:
ret = qemu_chr_fe_write(ibe->chr, ibe->outbuf + ibe->outpos,
                            ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos);
evidence.reason: The write consumes outbuf + outpos with length outlen - outpos. The only in-fragment producer of an invalid non-negative-length state is outpos += ret at line 11, and every path to it is preceded by the line-10 guard 'if (ret > 0)', which excludes ret <= 0 and therefore the standard negative-error return that would otherwise regress outpos before the next write. qemu_chr_fe_write's name-implied contract caps ret at the requested length, so the increment keeps outpos <= outlen, and any positive overshoot is reset at lines 19-20 before a later write. The capacity-dependent OOB arm is not assessable because no outbuf capacity appears in the fragment; a BLOCK-test witness for this sink cannot be produced. Resolution: PRESENT via line 10.

Decisive protective statement for the outpos/outlen invariant. Admitted set after the guard: ret in [1, outlen - outpos] (guard intersected with the callee's documented return bound), so outpos never decreases and never exceeds outlen; excluded set: ret <= 0, including the negative-error outcome that is the only standard failure reaching the accumulator. BREAK test: identity (same ret, no intervening modification), boundary (admitted maximum cannot exceed outlen - outpos), degenerate (0 and -1 excluded), reach (guard executes before the use on every path) — all pass. Resolution: PRESENT.

assumptions: qemu_chr_fe_write returns the number of bytes accepted in [0, len], negative on error, and never more than requested — standard, name-implied call-site semantics (callee body unshown).
outbuf, outlen, outpos are the IPMIBmcExtern struct fields named in the fragment; the struct per-type signedness and outbuf capacity are not shown in the fragment and are not assumed.
limitations: An out-of-bounds read of outbuf when outlen exceeds its (unshown) capacity is not assessable: no in-fragment declaration, allocation, or size expression establishes the capacity (CAPACITY-EVIDENCE RULE).
An entry-state inconsistency (outpos > outlen or outpos < 0) supplied by an unshown caller has no in-fragment producer, so it cannot support a BLOCK-test witness in either direction.
The outbuf[0] and outbuf[1] reset writes at lines 29-30 are fixed-index writes whose safety depends on an unshown capacity; demoted for lack of capacity evidence.

If the paired vulnerable member mutated outpos without the 'ret > 0' check, the shown fragment contains exactly the statement that excludes the negative-return regression; that membership observation was not used as verdict support.

verdict.summary: In FORMAT_INT's number path, the precision value prec is read from parsed format/parameter data with only a negative-to-(-1) clamp (L122-125) and no upper bound; the padding loop 'while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0';' (L207-208) then writes that many bytes backward from workend, past the start of the stack array 'char work[BUFFSIZE]' (L25), a stack-based buffer overflow reachable with e.g. prec=1000000.

evidence.reason: prec originates at L119 ('prec = (long)vto[p->precision].data.num.as_signed;') or L128 ('prec = p->precision;') with residual range {-1} U [0, LONG_MAX]; the only guards are the negative clamp L122-125 (excludes only prec<0, wrong-bound for the upper failure set) and L188-189 default. w starts at 'workend = &work[sizeof(work) - 2]' (L32) into 'char work[BUFFSIZE]' (L25); L198 only reduces prec by the digit count. A value such as prec=1000000 (from '%.1000000d') passes L205 ('if(prec > 0)') and drives 'while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0';' (L207-208) to write hundreds of thousands of bytes below &work[0] (CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow). Absent fix: clamp prec to the available space before the loop, e.g. 'if(prec > (long)(w - work)) prec = w - work;'. BLOCK test: no shown statement excludes the witness on the reaching path.

assumptions: work is a fixed-size stack array (L25); its writable span is work[0..sizeof(work)-1], with digits starting at &work[sizeof(work)-2] (L32).
The vto[] precision/parameter slots are filled by dprintf_Pass1 (L35) from format/ap_save, and the fragment's shown handling imposes no upper bound on the precision values it consumes.
limitations: Whether the format string itself is attacker-controlled depends on unshown callers; the verdict rests on the unconstrained residual range reaching the OOB write, per the analysis rules.

FORMAT_DOUBLE's '(sprintf)(work, formatbuf, p->data.dnum)' (L396) has width (L359-360) and precision (L376-377) clamps but may still write one byte (including sign/NUL) past 'work' for sign-flag plus maximum precision plus extreme value; treated as a weaker fragile-boundary candidate, not the decisive finding.
'p = &vto[param]' (L99) and 'f = *end++' (L423) assume dprintf_Pass1 bounds spec counts by MAX_PARAMETERS; not credited in either direction because its body is unshown.
Line 206 'width -= prec' can overflow long for extreme prec, but the L207-208 write overflow is already decisive.

verdict.summary: continue_send adds the return value of qemu_chr_fe_write directly to ibe->outpos with no error check. A standard negative return (failed chardev write) makes outpos negative; on the timer-driven retry (armed by the fragment itself), the call reads from ibe->outbuf + outpos and with length ibe->outlen - outpos, yielding an out-of-bounds read before the buffer.

evidence.snippet:
ibe->outpos += qemu_chr_fe_write(ibe->chr, ibe->outbuf + ibe->outpos,
                                     ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos);
evidence.reason: qemu_chr_fe_write's return value (standard chardev semantics: bytes written, or a negative error count) is added to outpos at line 7 with no negative check, producing outpos = -1 in the fragment itself. On the retry continuation armed at lines 11-12, the same statement indexes ibe->outbuf + (-1) and computes ibe->outlen - (-1) = outlen + 1, an out-of-bounds read before a buffer shown to contain at least indices 0 and 1 (line 26). The only guards en route are line 3 (excludes only outlen == 0, constrains the wrong variable) and line 9 (evaluated after the sink and admits negative outpos), so neither protects the call. Absent one-statement fix: capture the return and bail/reset on ret < 0 before outpos += ret. Mechanism: unchecked callee status lets a derived index go negative and be consumed by pointer arithmetic → CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: outlen/outpos behave as signed ints so a -1 accumulation stays negative (only then does the line-9 comparison admit the failing value; this matches the real vulnerable QEMU code for CVE-2018-17962).

ibe->extern_timer is bound to continue_send per standard QEMU timer-callback semantics; the fragment itself arms the retry at lines 11-12, and continue_send is the only consumer of the persistent outpos/outlen state.
ibe->outbuf has at least 2 elements because line 26 writes outbuf[1].
limitations: The capacity of ibe->outbuf is not declared in the fragment; the OOB is established via the in-fragment negative-index derivation (line 7) and the shown outbuf[0]/outbuf[1] accesses rather than a size literal.
If outlen/outpos were unsigned, a -1 return would wrap to a huge positive value and be absorbed by the else-branch reset at lines 15-16, so the verdict depends on the signed-field interpretation.

If the timer were not wired to continue_send (wiring outside the fragment), the negative outpos would not reappear at the sink within a single invocation; the fragment's own timer arming is the shown continuation.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in dprintf_formatf: an attacker-controlled precision value drives an unbounded zero-fill loop writing below the fixed-size work[BUFFSIZE] buffer.

evidence.reason: prec is a long derived from the format string (lines 118-130) with no shown upper bound, so its residual range is any positive value. The loop at line 207-208 executes prec times, decrementing w from workend = &work[sizeof(work)-2] (line 32), where work is char work[BUFFSIZE] (line 25). For any precision >= BUFFSIZE-1 (e.g. format '%.100000d'), w is written below work[0], a stack buffer overflow (CWE-787). The only guards on the path - if(prec > 0) at line 205 and prec -= (workend-w) at line 198 - admit or merely reduce prec but never cap it from above. The absent one-statement fix is a bound on prec (e.g. if(prec > BUFFSIZE) prec = BUFFSIZE;) or a bound keeping w within work. Witness survives the BLOCK test: no shown statement excludes a large prec before the write.

assumptions: work has the fixed capacity char work[BUFFSIZE] (line 25), with workend set to &work[sizeof(work)-2] (line 32).
prec for an integer conversion is derived from the format string via p->precision or vto[p->precision].data.num.as_signed with no shown maximum.
limitations: The FORMAT_DOUBLE formatbuf[32] writes (lines 347-379) also appear able to overflow, but confirmation depends on curl_msnprintf's return-value semantics and a specific combination of flags plus large width/precision, so it is not asserted as a second confirmed finding.

Attacker-controllability of the format string itself is not visible (no call site shown); the in-fragment consequence of an unconstrained precision reaching an unguarded write is the basis for the finding.
